ABSTRACT The aim of this study was to identify changes in photoplethysmogram waveform with
decreasing sampling frequency and quantization bit depth and suggest appropriate criteria for measurements.
We performed down-sampling and re-quantization of phoplethysmogram measured at high resolution.
Changes of waveform were quantitatively observed. Photoplethysmograms recorded at a 1-kHz sampling
frequency and 16-bit quantization bit depth were converted to signals with sampling frequencies of 500-,
250-, 100-, 50-, 25-, and 10-Hz by means of down-sampling. We then performed re-quantization to convert
the quantization bit depth into 16, 14, 12, 10, 8, and 6 bits for each down-sampled signal. Degradation
of signal was quantiﬁed in terms of morphological change and feature-point deviation. Morphological
analysis revealed that the correlation coefﬁcient was decreased while normalized root mean square error was
increased with decreasing sampling frequency and quantization bit depth. Feature-point analysis revealed
that the mean absolute time error and amplitude error of feature points tended to increase with decreasing
sampling frequency and quantization bit depth. Although there were differences according to pulse onset and
systolic peak, sampling frequency≥ 250-Hz and 16-bit quantization bits were required in order to have ≤
1 ms of timing error and a normalized amplitude error≤ 1%. In addition, sampling frequency≥ 100-Hz and
12-bit quantization bits are recommended to have feature-point time errors and amplitude errors < 10 ms
and a normalized amplitude error < 10%.
INDEX TERMS Analog-to-digital quantization bit depth, bio-signal measurement, photoplethysmogram,
sampling frequency.
I. INTRODUCTION
Photoplethysmography (PPG) is a non-invasive digital vol-
ume pulse measurement method based on an optical prin-
ciple that can monitor blood-volume changes and provide
cardiovascular information. A PPG system has a simple hard-
ware structure that is easy to implement. In addition, it can
be used to measure various body sites such as the wrist,
ﬁngertip, and earlobe. It can also be used for measurement
with a sensor without an electrode. Given its convenience,
PPG has already been applied on smartphones and smart
wearable devices such as the Samsung Galaxy (Samsung
Electronics, Inc., Suwon, Republic of Korea), Apple watch

(Apple, Inc., Cupertino, CA, USA), and MI band (Xiaomi,
Beijing, China). PPG can measure the amount of light trans-
mitted and reﬂected by irradiating the light on the periphery
of the human body according to light-absorbing properties
of hemoglobin in blood [1]. During cardiac systole, blood
is ejected from the heart into blood vessels, increasing the
blood volume of the vascular bed. However, during diastole,
the blood ﬂows from the blood vessel to the heart, thereby
decreasing the blood volume of the vascular bed. Since the
concentration of hemoglobin changes as the blood volume
changes, the amount of transmitted or reﬂected light changes,
resulting in a waveform that repeatedly rises and falls accord-
ing to the heartbeat in PPG [2].
PPG is widely used in clinical settings for monitoring heart
rate [3], [4], oxygen saturation [5], [6], respiration [7], [8],

and autonomic nervous system activation [9]–[12]. Heart rate
is calculated with the pulsation interval derived from PPG.
It can be used to assess rhythmic arrhythmia [3], [13] or
pulse changes according to exercise status [14], [15]. Oxygen
saturation is a percentage of oxyhemoglobin out of total
hemoglobin in the blood. It is calculated from the ratio of
red and infrared light absorbed by hemoglobin [16], [17].
In respiration, the respiration rate and the depth of respiration
can be measured by observing baseline changes or PPG pul-
sation interval variations of PPG [3], [4], [8]. PPG can also
be used to assess the autonomic nervous system. Similar to
heart-rate variability, autonomic nervous system changes can
be estimated from pulse-rate variations induced at pulse-to-
pulse interval in PPG [18]–[20]. In addition, autonomic ner-
vous system ﬂuctuations can be observed based on changes
of PPG amplitude, length, width, and height [13], [21]–[24]
in diastolic and systolic sections. Furthermore, blood pres-
sure [25], [26], cardiac output [27]–[29], arterial occlu-
sion [30], [31], surgical stress [32], [33], vascular aging
and arterial compliance [21], and hemodynamic and phys-
iological analyses using PPG have also been studied. Fig-
ure 1 shows various application ﬁelds of PPG.
PPG is mainly analyzed based on the waveform shape
or feature point of the waveform. When analyzing the PPG
waveform shape, one mainly observes changes in wave-
form according to physiological changes. For example,
morphological analysis of PPG can be used to analyze age-
ing effect [34], monitor nociception during general anesthe-
sia [23], and assess diabetes-associated arteriosclerosis [35].
In recent years, raw PPG has been applied to machine learn-
ing and analyzed without empirically observing waveforms
or features [36], [37]. When analyzing PPG based on fea-
ture points, intervals, amplitudes, and slopes between fea-
ture points are calculated to identify changes in each feature
according to a disease. In general, changes in peak interval are
known to reﬂect variations in the autonomic nervous system.
In addition, it has been reported that vascular characteristics
such as vascular aging and arterial compliance can be investi-
gated by changing the amplitude of feature points [38]–[40].
This analysis should presuppose that the PPG waveform is
obtained intact without distortion or deformation.
In the analog-to-digital conversion process, both sampling
rate and the quantization level play an important role in
preserving the raw signal without distortion. Preventing the
signal distortion is necessary since distortion in bio-signal
could lead fatal outcome in patient. Indeed, in some physi-
ological signal such as electrocardiogram (ECG), study for
optimal signal condition is studied and guideline was pro-
posed [41]. However, PPG has no relevant guidance and
only studies related to optimal sampling frequency was
reported [42], [43]. Devices commercially available from
different manufacturers have obtained PPG according to their
respective settings without speciﬁc guidelines. For example,
basic measurement methods such as sampling frequency and
quantization bit depth may be different for each measurement
device. Thus, the PPG obtained with each device may be
different. However, because of the limited capability of the
platform, most mobile devices need to minimize the amount
of computation and the amount of data to be stored. From this
point of view, lowering the sampling rate and quantization bit
depth is the most efﬁcient way to lower the computational
load. In this process, acquisition conditions in which wave-
form distortion is generated may be applied. Distortion and
deformation of the PPG waveform because of these acquisi-
tion conditions can lead to errors in analysis results. Previous
studies examining errors in PPG analysis based on sampling
frequency which is a basic acquisition condition have indi-
cated that acquisition of PPG with a sampling frequency <
25 Hz can cause fatal errors in pulse-rate variability analysis,
one of main applications of PPG [42]. Another study has
suggested that only some features can be considered commer-
cially usable if a sampling rate is lower than 30 Hz [43]. These
previous research studies have suggested a sampling con-
dition criterion for a speciﬁc application of PPG. However,
studies on acquisition conditions from a more universal point
of view covering the overall waveform change have not been
reported yet. Thus, the objective of this study was to quantify
changes of PPG according to changes of sampling frequency
and quantization bit depth for an in-depth examination of
universal PPG acquisition conditions. Speciﬁcally, changes
of PPG waveform and changes of positions of feature points
with decreased sampling frequency and the quantization bit
depth were quantitatively observed. Results of this study are
expected to provide guidelines for measurement methods that
ensure clinical signiﬁcance when measuring PPG in various
environments.
II. MATERIALS AND METHODS
The overall process of this study is shown in Fig. 2. The
obtained PPG signal was ﬁltered. Feature points were then
detected from the reference signal before down-sampling.
Degraded PPG signals were generated by down-sampling
and re-quantization. Thereafter, quantitative comparisons of
waveform changes and feature point positions between ref-
erence PPG and degraded PPG were performed, including
statistical analysis. Feature-point positions of degraded PPG
were detected and compared using detected feature-point
positions before degradation.

A. DATA MANIPULAION
We used dataset including PPG measured for 20 minutes from
30 participants without any reported disease. Two subjects’
data were excluded because of recording errors. Finally, data
from 28 subjects (20 males, 8 females, mean age of 22.0 ±
2.9 years) was used for analysis. All PPGs were measured
on a left index ﬁnger with a sampling frequency of 1 kHz.
They were measured over a voltage range of −10 V to
10 V with a measurement instrument and a 16-bit analog-to-
digital (ADC) converter. To record PPG, MP150, OXY100E,
and Acknowledge 4.0 (Biopac Systems, Santa Barbara, CA,
USA) were used for analog-digital conversion, PPG measure-
ment, and viewing and storing PPG to a computer, respec-
tively The obtained PPG was ﬁltered using a ﬁnite impulse
response bandpass ﬁlter with a 0.5-10 Hz passband.

quency and at 16-bit quantization bit depth. It was used as ref-
erence signal (PPG REF). Down-sampled PPG was generated
by decimation of PPG REF to have sampling frequencies of
500, 250, 100, 50, 25, and 10 Hz. Thereafter, down-sampled
